facts.statement: Fossils of Dryptosaurus were discovered by fertilizer miners in New Jersey within the New Egypt Formation.
facts.quote: These fossils were unearthed by fertilizer miners in New Jersey in rock layers of the New Egypt Formation.

facts.statement: The New Egypt Formation, where Dryptosaurus fossils were found, dates to the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 67 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: This formation dates to the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, around 67 to 66 million years ago.

facts.statement: Unlike larger tyrannosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus and Tarbosaurus, Dryptosaurus had large forelimbs with big claws and slender hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Size estimates for Dryptosaurus range from 7.5 meters in length and 756 to 1500 kilograms in mass.
facts.quote: Size estimates place it at 7.5 m in length and 756 - 1500 kg in mass.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus possessed ziphodont dentition, characterized by sharp, blade-like, laterally compressed teeth, which differs from larger tyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: The genus had ziphodont (sharp, blade-like, laterally compressed) dentition, dissimilar to that of larger tyrannosaurs.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is classified as a member of the clade Eutyrannosauria, which includes Tyrannosauridae and genera like Nanotyrannus and Bistahieversor.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus is a member of Eutyrannosauria, the clade including Tyrannosauridae and tyrannosaurs like Nanotyrannus and Bistahieversor but excluding more basal tyrannosaurs like Dilong.

facts.statement: Some studies suggest Dryptosaurus may belong to its own family, Dryptosauridae, or to the family Nanotyrannidae.
facts.quote: However, some studies have also put it in its own family, Dryptosauridae, or in Nanotyrannidae.

facts.statement: In the summer of 1866, workers from the West Jersey Marl Company uncovered a theropod skeleton near Barnsboro, New Jersey, in the New Egypt Formation.
facts.quote: During the summer of 1866, workers from the West Jersey Marl Company uncovered an associated theropod skeleton in sediments coming from the New Egypt Formation in a quarry near Barnsboro, New Jersey.

facts.statement: On August 21, 1866, Edward Drinker Cope formally named the specimen Laelaps aquilunguis before presenting it to the American Philosophical Society.
facts.quote: On 21 August 1866, Cope presented his description of ANSP 9995 to the American Philosophical Society at what is now the Academy of Natural Sciences, naming it a new genus and species of dinosaur, Laelaps aquilunguis.

facts.statement: In 1877, Othniel Charles Marsh renamed the genus Dryptosaurus because the original name Laelaps was already used for a mite.
facts.quote: In 1877, Marsh pointed out that Cope's genus name Laelaps was preoccupied by a genus of mite, leading to Marsh to erect the genus name Dryptosaurus.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope continued to use the name Laelaps for the dinosaur despite Othniel Charles Marsh's replacement with Dryptosaurus.
facts.quote: Despite this, Cope continued to use the name Laelaps, refusing to use Dryptosaurus.

facts.statement: Several sacral vertebrae originally assigned to Dryptosaurus by Cope are now thought to belong to the turtle species Pneumatoarthrus.
facts.quote: Several sacral vertebrae Cope assigned to Dryptosaurus are now believed to belong to the protostegid turtle Pneumatoarthrus.

facts.statement: An isolated metatarsal found near the original site is possibly part of the Dryptosaurus skeleton, but this attribution is uncertain.
facts.quote: An isolated metatarsal IV (AMNH FARB 2438) possibly belonging to ANSP 9995 was found at the same locale, but this has come into question.

facts.statement: Well-preserved casts of most Dryptosaurus type material are currently held at the Natural History Museum in London.
facts.quote: Brusatte et al. (2011) noted that well-preserved, historic casts of most of the type material from ANSP 9995 and AMNH FARB 2438 are housed in the collections of the Natural History Museum in London (NHM OR50100).

facts.statement: Oramel W. Lucas discovered Laelaps trihedrodon between 1877 and 1878 in the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: Laelaps trihedrodon was first discovered by Oramel W. Lucas, a schoolteacher from Garden Park, Colorado, who collected an incomplete dentary with teeth from 1877 to 1878 in strata of the Late Jurassic-aged Morrison Formation in Garden Park.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described Laelaps trihedrodon as a new species in 1877.
facts.quote: Cope described this material as belonging to a new species of Laelaps, Laelaps trihedrodon, "three-hedged tooth", in 1877.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named Dryptosaurus macropus in 1868 based on fossils from New Jersey.
facts.quote: In 1868 Cope described this specimen (AMNH 2550-2553) as belonging to its own species of Laelaps (Dryptosaurus) which he named L. macropus.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named Laelaps falculus in 1876 based on teeth from the Late Cretaceous Judith River Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1876, Cope named Laelaps falculus on the basis of ten isolated teeth that had been found by Jno. C. Issac from the "Fort Union Beds" (now considered the Judith River Formation) of Montana dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named Laelaps incrassatus in 1876 based on teeth from the Late Cretaceous Judith River Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1876, Cope named Laelaps incrassatus on the basis of two isolated maxillary teeth that had been found by Jno. C. Issac from the "Fort Union Beds" (now considered the Judith River Formation) of Montana dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named Laelaps explanatus in 1876 based on teeth from the Late Cretaceous Judith River Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1876, Cope named Laelaps explanatus on the basis of several teeth that had been found in rocks of the "Fort Union Beds" (now considered the Judith River Formation) of Montana dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described Laelaps hazenianus in 1876 from the Late Cretaceous Judith River Group of Montana.
facts.quote: Laelaps hazenianus was described by Cope in 1876 on the basis of seven teeth from the Judith River Group of Montana dating to the Late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope assigned tyrannosaur skulls from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta to Laelaps incrassatus in 1892.
facts.quote: In 1892, Cope assigned two incomplete tyrannosaur skulls from rocks of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, Canada to L. incrassatus on the basis of their similar tooth anatomy.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe named Dryptosaurus incrassatus in 1903 and 1904, but the skulls are now assigned to Albertosaurus sarcophagus.
facts.quote: In 1903 and 1904, Lawrence Lambe used the valid generic name Dryptosaurus incrassatus for the skulls, however both of these skulls are now assigned to Albertosaurus sarcophagus, while L. incrassatus is considered a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Donald Baird and John R. Horner described fossils from the Campanian-aged Tar Heel/Coachman Formation in North Carolina in 1979.
facts.quote: In 1979, Donald Baird and John R. Horner described a multitude of fossils from the Campanian-aged Tar Heel/Coachman Formation in North Carolina, United States.

facts.statement: Chase Brownstein tentatively classified partial teeth and femur fragments as Dryptosaurus aquilunguis in February 2018.
facts.quote: In February 2018, based on specimens described by Baird and Horner (1979), Brownstein tentatively classified the partial teeth (USNM 7199 and ANSP 15332) as D. sp. and the partial femur fragments (ANSP 15330 and USNM 7189, the latter of which was in part a syntype of Hypsibema) as D. aquilunguis.

facts.statement: A 2018 paper tentatively assigned teeth from the Maastrichtian-aged Marshalltown Formation in New Jersey to Dryptosaurus.
facts.quote: A 2018 paper tentatively assigned two isolated teeth from the Ellisdale Site in Monmouth County, New Jersey, which contains strata of the Maastrichthian-aged Marshalltown Formation, to Dryptosaurus.

facts.statement: David Chure argued in 2001 that fossil AMNH 5780 likely belongs to Allosaurus rather than Laelaps trihedrodon.
facts.quote: In 2001, Chure argued that AMNH 5780 probably belongs to Allosaurus.

facts.statement: Chase Brownstein argued in 2017 that Teihivenator macropus is a chimera and a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: In 2017, Chan-gyu Yun informally gave it the new generic name Teihivenator, stating that it was its own genus of tyrannosauroid. However that same year Chase Brownstein argued that "Teihivenator macropus" is actually a chimera and a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Laelaps falculus represents a distinct species, with some suggesting it is based on juvenile tyrannosaur teeth.

facts.statement: Laelaps incrassatus is currently considered a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: Research indicates that some tyrannosauroid teeth from New Jersey are more similar to Appalachiosaurus than to Dryptosaurus.
